core: History is the evidence-based study and interpretation of the human past, and it is not identical to the past itself: the past is everything that happened, while history is the account historians reconstruct and write from surviving evidence
The historian's research process: asking a focused historical question, finding and evaluating sources, interpreting the evidence, and constructing a supported argument or narrative

Historiography: historical interpretations are written by people and change over time as new evidence, new questions, and new perspectives emerge, so there can be competing scholarly accounts of the same events

Sources are the raw materials of the craft: primary sources come from the time under study, secondary sources retell, analyze, or interpret it, and both must be read critically (author, audience, intent, context)
History's relationship to neighboring evidence-based fields such as archaeology, named only briefly
supporting: The AHA 'five C's' vocabulary (change over time, context, causality, contingency, complexity) as the shared conceptual habits historians use to build arguments — named as the discipline's thinking, with the skills owned by the sibling historical-thinking topic
History is interpretive: causality and meaning are argued from partial evidence, so historians can disagree without either being simply wrong
Analyzing a source moves from observation to questioning to reasoned inference, not from copying a source's claims
outOfScope: The historical-thinking skills themselves in depth — sourcing, contextualization, corroboration, close reading (owned by history:foundations:historical-thinking)
Primary sources as a full topic — types, strengths, and limits (owned by history:foundations:primary-sources)
Secondary sources as a full topic (owned by history:foundations:secondary-sources)
Evidence-and-interpretation and bias-and-perspective as full topics (their own siblings)
Any specific historical period, event, or civilization's narrative content

claims.claim: History is the disciplined, evidence-based study and interpretation of the human past; it is distinct from the past itself, because the past is everything that happened while history is the reconstructed account historians build and write from surviving evidence.

Historians work by gathering as much evidence as they can and then interpreting it to draw conclusions; because sources are partial, causality and meaning are argued rather than simply read off the record.

Primary sources are the raw materials of history, created at the time under study, and are distinct from secondary sources, which retell, analyze, or interpret events usually at a distance of time or place; analyzing a source moves from observation to questioning to reasoned inference.
Interpreting a primary source requires attention to its author, audience, intent, and context, rather than taking its statements at face value.

Historiography — the writing and rewriting of history — is central to the discipline: historians continually reevaluate and revise earlier interpretations because the people doing history, the questions they ask, and the sources and tools available to them change over time, so the same event can carry different meanings from different vantage points.

The American Historical Association's 'five C's of historical thinking' — change over time, context, causality, contingency, and complexity — describe the shared conceptual habits historians use to formulate and support arguments from primary sources and to evaluate the interpretations in secondary sources.

History is one of several evidence-based fields that study the human past; it overlaps with disciplines such as archaeology, and historians increasingly work in a multidisciplinary way, drawing on many kinds of data beyond written documents.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How firmly to state that history is 'objective' versus 'interpretive'.
positions: Popular usage treats history as a fixed set of facts about what happened

Professional practice (AHA, NCPH, OpenStax) treats established facts and their interpretation as different layers: what happened can be well established while why it happened and what it meant remain open to argument and revision
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson distinguishes established facts (what/when) from interpretation (why/meaning), presents historiographical change as normal scholarly practice rather than as history being 'unreliable', and never both-sides the occurrence of documented events.

sourceRecords.title: What Does It Mean to Think Historically?
sourceRecords.notes: Thomas Andrews and Flannery Burke, January 2007. Supports the 'five C's of historical thinking' (change over time, context, causality, contingency, complexity), that historians interpret partial primary sources to build arguments about causality and meaning, and that these habits are used to formulate arguments from primary sources and to challenge interpretations in secondary sources. Verified via WebFetch 2026-08-19. AHA-copyrighted; facts verified, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: World History Volume 1, to 1500, Section 1.2: Primary Sources

sourceRecords.title: Getting Started with Primary Sources
sourceRecords.notes: Defines primary sources as 'the raw materials of history — original documents and objects that were created at the time under study,' distinct from secondary sources that 'retell, analyze, or interpret events, usually at a distance of time or place,' and describes analysis as moving from observation to questioning, evaluating information, making inferences, and developing reasoned interpretations. U.S. government work; text in the public domain. Live page blocked the fetcher (Cloudflare); verified via an Internet Archive capture read with curl on 2026-08-19.

sourceRecords.title: The Changing Past
sourceRecords.notes: Supports historiography: the people doing history, the questions they ask, and the tools and materials available are anything but static, so historians continually reevaluate and revise earlier interpretations; the same event (e.g., 1492) can look very different from different vantage points, making history a task of interpreting rather than simply collecting data. © NCPH, All Rights Reserved; REFERENCE_ONLY.
